title: 5 AI Prompts Every Professional Should Save

scenes.badge: Average length of the most successful prompts
scenes.sub: Google's Gemini for Workspace Prompting Guide 101 (April 2024)
scenes.text: Here's a number that explains a lot about bad AI answers. Google's prompting guide for Gemini in Workspace says the most successful prompts average around twenty one words. But the prompts people usually try are short, often less than nine words. That gap is why so many AI answers feel generic. In this video, I'll give you five prompts every professional should save, built from the official prompting guides from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. Each one is a template you can copy, fill in, and reuse every week, whichever chatbot you use.

scenes.chapterTitle: How often people really use AI at work

footer.text: Most people are still occasional users

scenes.text: First, some context. In a Gallup survey of more than twenty two thousand US workers, reported by the Associated Press in January twenty twenty six, twelve percent said they use AI daily in their job. Roughly a quarter use it at least a few times a week, and nearly half use it at least a few times a year. So most people are still occasional users. And when you only use a tool now and then, you start from a blank box every time. Saved prompts fix that.

items.text: Persona: who the AI should act as
Task: the exact job, as a verb

footer.text: Brief it like a new hire

scenes.text: All five templates use the same simple formula. Google's guide names four areas: persona, task, context and format. Persona is who the AI should act as. Task is the exact job, written as a verb, like summarize or draft. Context is the facts it can't guess, like who the audience is. Format is the length, layout and tone you want. Anthropic's guide puts it another way: treat the AI like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms. If a new colleague would be confused by your request, the AI will be too.

items.name: Persona
items.desc: You are my chief of staff

footer.text: Turns a long read into a 1-minute brief

scenes.text: Prompt one is the Briefing. Use it for long reports, contracts, or email threads. Here it is. You are my chief of staff. Summarize the document below for a busy manager. Give me three key points, any decisions I need to make, every deadline mentioned, and open questions. Keep it under one hundred fifty words. If something is unclear or missing, say so instead of guessing. Then paste the document. That last line matters, because it gives the AI permission to admit gaps rather than fill them in. You get a one minute brief instead of a twenty minute read.

items.name: Persona
items.desc: Act as a clear, polite professional

items.name: Task
items.desc: Draft a reply to the email below

items.name: Context
items.desc: My goal, my answer, the relationship

items.name: Format
items.desc: Under 120 words, friendly, one clear ask

footer.text: You still read it before you hit send

scenes.text: Prompt two is the Reply Drafter, for the emails you keep putting off. Act as a clear, polite professional. Draft a reply to the email below. My goal is, and then one line, like decline the meeting but offer Thursday. My answer is, and the key facts. The relationship is, for example a client I want to keep. Keep it under one hundred twenty words, friendly but direct, with one clear ask at the end. OpenAI's own guide suggests naming the tone with descriptive words, like friendly or firm. And always read the draft before you hit send.

items.text: What does a great result look like?
What must it include or avoid?

scenes.text: Prompt three is the most underrated: Interview Me First. Use it when you don't know what context to give. Here it is. I need help with, and then the task, like a project proposal. Before you write anything, ask me up to five questions, one at a time, about what you need to know to do this well. Only then write the first draft. The AI will ask things like who is this for, what does a great result look like, and what must it include or avoid. Instead of you guessing what context matters, the AI pulls it out of you.

items.text: Say what is missing or unclear

footer.text: Get the hard questions before your boss asks

scenes.text: Prompt four is the Critic. Most people ask AI to write. Fewer ask it to push back, and that's often more useful. Act as a skeptical decision maker who has to approve this. Review my draft below. List the five weakest points, say what is missing or unclear, and suggest one specific fix for each. Don't rewrite the whole thing. Use it on a pitch, a report, or a slide outline before it goes out. You'll hear the hard questions before your boss or client asks them, while there's still time to fix them.

items.name: Task
items.desc: Turn these meeting notes into actions

items.name: Flag
items.desc: Any task with no owner or no date

footer.text: Messy notes in, clear next steps out

scenes.text: Prompt five is Notes to Actions. Paste in rough meeting notes or a transcript and use this. Turn these meeting notes into a table with four columns: action, owner, deadline, and status. Use only what's written in the notes. Flag any task that has no owner or no date. Then write a three line follow up email I can send to the team. The words use only what's written are important, because they stop the AI from inventing owners or dates that nobody agreed to. Messy notes go in, clear next steps come out.

footer.text: You type it once, then reuse it

scenes.text: Here's the difference side by side. A typical prompt is, summarize this report. Three words. The AI has to guess who you are, what you care about, and how long the answer should be. The Briefing template is over forty words, and it answers all of those questions up front. That's well above the twenty one word average Google saw in successful prompts. And here's the point of saving them: you only type it once. After that, it takes about five seconds to paste, fill in the brackets, and go.

items.name: Iterate
items.desc: Review the answer, then refine the prompt

items.name: Show examples
items.desc: Anthropic suggests 3 to 5 for best results

items.name: Question last
items.desc: Paste long docs first, ask at the end

scenes.text: Four tips from the official guides make these templates even better. One, iterate. OpenAI and Google both say to review the answer and refine your prompt, like a conversation. Two, show examples. If you want a certain style, paste a sample. Anthropic's guide suggests three to five examples for best results. Three, tell the AI what to do instead of only what not to do. Write in short paragraphs works better than don't use bullet points. Four, with long documents, paste the document first and put your question at the end.

items.name: Check your policy
items.desc: Follow your company's rules on AI tools

items.name: Protect private data
items.desc: Remove names, numbers and client details

items.name: Verify facts
items.desc: AI can sound sure and still be wrong

scenes.text: Before you use these at work, three rules. First, check your company's policy on AI tools. Many employers say which tools are approved and what you can paste into them. Second, protect private data. Remove names, account numbers and client details unless your company's approved tool allows them. Third, verify facts. AI can sound confident and still be wrong, especially with numbers, dates and quotes. That's why two of the templates tell the AI to flag gaps instead of guessing. The AI drafts. You decide what goes out.

scenes.chapterTitle: How to save your prompt library

items.text: A text shortcut to paste fast

footer.text: Your best prompts become a tool

scenes.text: Finally, how to actually save them so you use them. Create one note or document called Prompt Library. Paste all five templates in, and put square brackets around the parts you change, like the document or your goal. If you want to go faster, a text expander or your phone's text replacement can paste a whole template from a short shortcut. And once a week, improve one prompt based on what went wrong. Over a month, your best prompts stop being one off messages and become a tool you trust.

scenes.title: Save these 5 today

scenes.text: So, your five prompts: the Briefing, the Reply Drafter, Interview Me First, the Critic, and Notes to Actions. All of them follow one formula: persona, task, context and format. Which prompt do you use most at work? Share it in the comments. I read them, and the best ones might end up in a future video. If this helped, subscribe to Future Money Lab. Next up, AI for Excel and Google Sheets: how to turn hours of spreadsheet work into minutes.

youtube.title: 5 AI Prompts Every Professional Should Save (Free Templates)
youtube.summary: Five copy-paste AI prompt templates for work that you can use with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or any chatbot: the Briefing (summarize any document), the Reply Drafter (emails), Interview Me First (let the AI ask the questions), the Critic (find weak points before your boss does) and Notes to Actions (meeting notes into an action table). All five are built on the 4-part formula from Google's prompting guide (persona, task, context, format) plus tips from OpenAI's and Anthropic's official guides, with 3 rules for using AI safely at work.
youtube.details:
Numbers and sources mentioned (checked November 2026):
- The most successful prompts average around 21 words; prompts people often try are usually less than nine words (Google, Gemini for Google Workspace Prompting Guide 101, April 2024 edition).
- 12% of employed US adults use AI daily in their job; roughly one-quarter at least a few times a week; nearly half at least a few times a year (Gallup Workforce survey of 22,368 US workers, Oct 30 - Nov 13, 2025, as reported by the Associated Press, January 2026).
- Persona, task, context and format: the four areas in Google's guide.
- 'Brilliant but new employee' and '3-5 examples for best results': Anthropic's Claude prompting best practices.
- Iterate and refine; describe the tone with descriptive words: OpenAI Help Center, Prompt engineering best practices for ChatGPT.
- The five templates are our own, built from these guides; they are suggestions, not measured results. '3 vs 40+ words' compares our example prompts.
- Always follow your employer's AI policy and verify AI output.
